summary: Reviewed the full dvpwa (aiohttp) Python web application: DAO layer (sqli/dao/*), views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app bootstrap, config, and Jinja2 templates. The app is intentionally vulnerable and the code confirms several high-impact, reachable flaws: a classic SQL injection in Student.create, application-wide XSS caused by disabling Jinja2 autoescaping, disabled CSRF protection, weak unsalted MD5 password hashing, and a session cookie exposed to JavaScript. Static assets (materialize/jquery) were not audited. Overall risk is critical.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via unparameterized name interpolation
findings.description: The student name is concatenated directly into the INSERT statement using Python % string formatting instead of a parameterized query. The value flows unsanitized from the HTTP POST body: views.students() (POST /students/) reads data['name'] and passes it to Student.create(conn, data['name']). The students POST handler performs no authentication check, so any anonymous user can inject arbitrary SQL. An attacker can break out of the quoted VALUES string to run stacked/subquery SQL, read or modify arbitrary tables (e.g. users/pwd_hash), or destroy data.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); cur.execute(q)  <- name comes from request.post()['name'] in views.py:55-57. Example payload name = x'); DROP TABLE students;-- . Contrast with Course.create/Mark.create/Review.create which correctly pass params to cur.execute().
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with % / f-strings / concatenation from user input.

findings.title: Stored XSS from Jinja2 autoescape disabled application-wide
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every template expression renders raw HTML unless a manual | e filter is applied. Several templates output attacker-controlled, persisted data without escaping, producing stored XSS reachable by any visitor. Course reviews (review_text) are created from unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review and rendered raw in course.jinja2 (line 22); course titles/descriptions are rendered raw in course.jinja2 (lines 14-15) and student.jinja2 (lines 19-20); student names are rendered raw in students.jinja2 (line 16) and course.jinja2 (line 49). Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, an injected script can steal sessions.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example course.jinja2:22 '{{ review.review_text }}' <- Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) <- data.get('review_text') in views.py:121-129.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2']) or autoescape=True) and remove reliance on manual | e filters; escape or sanitize all user-controlled output.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled (csrf_middleware not registered)
findings.description: A working CSRF middleware exists (middlewares.csrf_middleware) and templates emit _csrf_token hidden fields, but the middleware is commented out of the application middleware chain, so no state-changing POST request's CSRF token is ever validated. All mutating endpoints (login POST /, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker page can, e.g., force an authenticated admin to create records or an anonymous victim to submit data.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware in middlewares.py:25-38 validates session token vs formdata['_csrf_token'] but is never added.
findings.recommendation: Register csrf_middleware in the middlewares list so all POST handlers enforce the token check.

findings.title: Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing in User.check_password
findings.description: Password verification compares the stored hash to md5(password). Passwords are hashed with a single round of unsalted MD5, which is fast and broken for password storage: if the user table leaks (e.g. via the SQL injection above), hashes are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/brute force. The equality comparison is also non-constant-time.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(). Fixtures/migrations store md5 hashes consumed here.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hashing algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2) and a constant-time comparison. Migrate existing hashes on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis-backed session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is accessible to client-side JavaScript. Together with the application-wide XSS (autoescape disabled), this lets an injected script read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, enabling full session hijacking. No Secure flag is set either, allowing transmission over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Create the storage with httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True / an appropriate SameSite policy for the session cookie.

findings.title: aiohttp application started with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True, which enables verbose diagnostics (e.g. unclosed-resource warnings, more detailed error behavior) and is not appropriate for production. Shipped with the plaintext error handling it can aid information disclosure to attackers.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.
